section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from December 1946 to July 1949 concerning labor unrest, strikes, and strike prohibitions in Allied-occupied Japan. A major portion details the planned February 1, 1947 general strike of government and public office workers, which was averted by General Douglas MacArthur's intervention and generated extensive diplomatic reporting, petitions, and Allied debate. Subsequent documents address the July 1948 restrictions on civil service strikes, the June 1949 National Railway workers' strike in the Tokyo-Yokohama area, and the political tensions surrounding the Yoshida administration's implementation of the U.S.-directed economic stabilization program.

subfiles.about: Outgoing telegram repeating a Moscow report to the Political Adviser in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: State Department repeats Moscow telegram 4307 of December 3 to SCAP Tokyo for information.
subfiles.title: Telegram 596 to SCAP Tokyo Repeating Moscow Telegram 4307
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Airgram reporting British parliamentary questions regarding General MacArthur's prohibition of the Japanese general strike.
subfiles.summary: Transmits House of Commons exchange wherein Christopher Mayhew affirms SCAP's authority under Far Eastern Commission policy to prohibit strikes prejudicial to occupation objectives.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-400 from London on House of Commons Debate on Japanese Labor Strike

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the planned February 1, 1947 general strike in Japan prohibited by General MacArthur, with attached statements, petitions, and press comments.
keywords: National Government and Public Office Workers Union
subfiles.summary: The United States Political Adviser reports that a planned general strike by Japanese government and public office workers was averted when General MacArthur issued an order prohibiting it on January 31, 1947. While the workers' original grievances stemmed from severe post-war inflation and food shortages, the strike movement became increasingly politicized under Communist and left-wing leadership. Transmitted with the despatch are MacArthur's prohibition statement, union representations and petitions to Allied authorities, intelligence check sheets, and Japanese press commentaries reflecting broad relief at the strike's cancellation.
subfiles.title: Despatch 889 on Proposed General Strike Planned to Begin on February 1, 1947

subfiles.about: Airgram reporting British parliamentary debate on labor conditions and Commonwealth representation on the Allied Council for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Transmits British House of Commons questions to Minister of State Hector McNeil concerning trade union conditions in Japan, SCAP supervision, and Allied Council consultation.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-540 from London on House of Commons Inquiry Concerning Japanese Labor Conditions

subfiles.about: Airgram summarizing a Soviet newspaper article attacking American occupation policy and praising Communist labor agitation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes a Soviet trade union newspaper article accusing the United States of suppressing Japanese labor, exempting Zaibatsu trusts, and collaborating with right-wing Socialists.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-361 from Moscow Reporting Trud Article on the Strike Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram relaying a Chinese news report on Osaka government workers petitioning Allied missions against strike bans.
subfiles.summary: Relays a Central News Agency report describing how 82,000 Osaka government workers petitioned Allied missions in Tokyo against the Ashida Cabinet's no-strike ordinance and police suppression.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1797 from Shanghai on Osaka Government Workers' Petition Against No-Strike Ordinance

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Secretary of State Marshall and British Foreign Secretary Bevin concerning Japanese strike prohibitions.
subfiles.summary: British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin suggests providing arbitration machinery for Japanese civil servants deprived of the right to strike, noting similar concerns raised by American labor.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Japanese Labor Law Prohibiting Civil Service Strikes

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Soviet press coverage of the Japanese Diet considering revisions to government worker strike prohibitions.
subfiles.summary: Reports a Pravda item stating the Japanese Lower House agreed to review the law depriving government employees of the right to strike.
subfiles.title: Telegram 2809 from Moscow on Pravda Report Concerning Japanese Strike Legislation

subfiles.about: Memorandum forwarding an intelligence research study on the Japanese railroad strike and commenting on Prime Minister Yoshida's labor policies.
subfiles.summary: Transmits DRF's study on the railway strike, questioning whether Yoshida would turn anti-Communist measures into an anti-labor campaign.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum Transmitting DRF Study on the Japanese Railway Strike

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing the Communist-inspired Kanagawa railway strike and SCAP's direct intervention to restore rail service.
subfiles.summary: Details how SCAP promptly quashed a Communist-led strike on the Tokyo-Yokohama lines protesting personnel retrenchment during Kato Etsuo's absence in Paris.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum on Strike by Certain Japanese Government Railways Workers

subfiles.about: Comprehensive intelligence report analyzing the causes, Communist leadership, government response, and political implications of the June 1949 Japanese railway strike.
subfiles.from: Division of Research for Far East, Office of Intelligence Research
subfiles.summary: This intelligence report examines the June 1949 Tokyo-area government railway strike precipitated by mass layoff plans under the U.S.-directed economic stabilization program. While initiated over new work schedules, the dispute reflected militant leftist resistance by the Communist-led Kokutetsu leadership against statutory personnel retrenchments. The analysis warns that Prime Minister Yoshida might exploit anti-Communist sentiment to launch a broader anti-labor offensive, potentially alienating moderate labor and undermining political stability.
subfiles.title: OIR Report No. 5002: Japan: The Railroad Strike of June 9-12 and Its Aftermath

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing radio intercepts regarding the dismissal of railway strike leaders and Prime Minister Yoshida's conciliatory public speech.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes Tokyo intercepts indicating the railway strike collapsed following dismissals of leftist committee members, while Yoshida adopted a calmer, SCAP-influenced tone.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum on Developments in Japanese Strike Situation

subfiles.about: Memorandum submitting a draft cable to SCAP regarding allegations of slave labor in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Transmits draft cable to SCAP concerning slave labor reports, noting War Department concurrence and subsequent telephone amendments.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum on Report of Slave Labor in Japan
